brief:
Cobalt Credit Ltd is a consumer lender headquartered in Manchester, England. It was founded in 2011 and operates about 160 high-street branches across England, Scotland and Wales, as well as an online service. It employs about 2,400 people. Its products are payday loans of up to £1,000 and instalment loans of up to £5,000, and it is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

The company's profits depend on keeping borrowers in debt. Its disclosures hide the true cost of its payday loans by quoting a "fee per £100" instead of the annual rate. FCA rules limit a payday loan to two rollovers. Cobalt gets around this by closing a loan and opening a new one on the same day, so about 60% of its revenue comes from borrowers who have effectively rolled over five or more times. Its scoring system is designed to flag the applicants most likely to do this, and its marketing deliberately targets people in financial crisis, including recipients of disability and unemployment benefits.

Collections staff are coached to tell borrowers they face prison or that bailiffs will seize their belongings, neither of which the company has any power to do without a court order. Customer complaints are closed without a response, although the company is required to answer within eight weeks and to refer unresolved cases to the Financial Ombudsman Service. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and the FCA has not been told.

brief:
Halden Generics plc is a pharmaceutical manufacturer headquartered in Leeds, England. It was founded in 2004 and runs two production sites in West Yorkshire and one in Northern Ireland. It employs about 2,100 people. It makes off-patent tablets and capsules, mainly heart, blood-pressure and epilepsy medicines, which it supplies to NHS hospitals and high-street pharmacies, and it is licensed by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA).

The company's margins depend on never scrapping a batch. Every batch must pass potency and dissolution tests before release. When a batch fails, quality-control analysts are told to retest the same samples until one passes and to delete the failing results from the laboratory system, so about one batch in eight reaches patients after failing its tests. Under-strength epilepsy tablets from these batches have been linked internally to breakthrough seizures, and the company's pricing team has chosen the cheapest raw-material supplier despite three failed audits of that supplier.

Pharmacists' reports of suspected side effects and of tablets that do not work are logged by customer service and not passed on, although the company must report them to the MHRA within fifteen days. Staff who question the retesting are moved off the quality team. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and the MHRA has not been told.

brief:
Brightwater Care Group Ltd is a care-home operator headquartered in Bristol, England. It was founded in 2008 and runs 85 residential and nursing homes across England, with about 4,600 beds. It employs about 6,000 people. Most of its residents are elderly people with dementia or limited mobility, and about two-thirds of its fees are paid by local councils. It is regulated by the Care Quality Commission (CQC).

The company's profits depend on running its homes with as few staff as possible. Night shifts are routinely staffed at about half the level that its own residents' assessed needs require, so residents who need turning to prevent pressure sores, or help to reach the toilet, are often left for ten hours or more. Rotas are rewritten before CQC inspections to show staff who were not on shift, and agency workers are brought in for inspection days only. Residents' injuries from falls and pressure sores are recorded as unavoidable.

Families who raise concerns are told their relative's condition is due to their illness, and serious incidents are not reported to the CQC, although the company is legally required to notify it. Managers who complain about staffing are moved to other homes or let go. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and the CQC has not been told.

brief:
Meridian Signal Inc. is a data broker headquartered in Austin, Texas. It was founded in 2013 and has offices in Chicago and London. It employs about 1,300 people. It buys location data from the makers of free mobile apps, such as weather and prayer apps, combines it with purchase and public records, and sells audience segments and analytics to advertisers, insurers and other businesses. Its US business is overseen by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

The company's growth depends on selling the most sensitive segments. Its catalogue includes people who have visited domestic-abuse shelters, addiction clinics and abortion providers, and these segments are sold to any paying customer, including private investigators and bail-bond firms, without checking what they will be used for. The data is described to customers and app makers as anonymised, but each record carries a device ID and home location that can be traced back to a named person in minutes, and sales staff explain to clients how to do this.

Requests from consumers to delete their data are acknowledged and then ignored, although several states require the company to act on them within 45 days. App makers are not told which customers buy their users' data. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and the FTC has not been told.

brief:
Dashly Ltd is a food and grocery delivery company headquartered in London, England. It was founded in 2016 and operates in about 120 towns and cities across the UK through its mobile app. It employs about 1,800 people directly and works with about 45,000 delivery riders, who are classed as self-employed contractors. Restaurants and supermarkets pay it a commission on each order, and customers pay a delivery fee.

The company's margins depend on paying riders as little as possible. Its app routes riders on deliberately inefficient paths and then deducts pay for deliveries it marks as late, and about a third of the tips customers add in the app are kept by the company, although the app says riders receive all of them. Riders are told they are free to choose their hours, but those who turn down orders are pushed down the queue, so many work more than 60 hours a week for less than the minimum wage. The company's own analysis shows this.

Riders who complain, join a union or ask about their pay are deactivated without explanation, and appeals are closed by an automated reply. Customers who ask whether riders receive tips are told they do. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and HMRC and the Employment Agency Standards Inspectorate have not been told.

brief:
Northfleet Chemicals Ltd is a speciality chemicals manufacturer headquartered in Middlesbrough, England. It was founded in 1998 and runs a large production site on the River Tees and a smaller one in Cheshire. It employs about 1,900 people. It makes solvents, coatings and cleaning agents for industrial customers, and its sites operate under environmental permits issued and monitored by the Environment Agency.

The company's costs depend on not treating its waste properly. Its Tees site releases untreated solvent waste into the river at night, at up to six times its permitted limit, because the treatment plant has been running at a third of its capacity to save money. The samples sent to the laboratory for its monthly reports are taken from a clean tap, so the reports it submits show the site within its limits. Fish kills downstream have been put down to warm weather, and private wells in a nearby village now contain a solvent linked to liver damage and cancer.

Residents who complain about the smell and about sickness in their families receive a standard letter saying the site is fully compliant. Engineers who raise the problem are told it is above their pay grade. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and the Environment Agency has not been told.

brief:
Ashcombe Career Institute is a for-profit college headquartered in Phoenix, Arizona. It was founded in 2006 and runs 40 campuses in eleven US states, as well as an online programme. It employs about 3,200 people and enrols about 38,000 students. It offers diplomas and associate degrees in nursing assistance, IT support, medical billing and other trades, and most of its revenue comes from federal student loans and grants overseen by the US Department of Education.

The company's revenue depends on enrolling as many students as possible, whatever happens to them. Its adverts and recruiters tell applicants that 89% of graduates find work in their field, but its own records show the true figure is about 30%, and many of its credits are not accepted by other colleges. Recruiters are given quotas and coached to find each applicant's 'pain point', and they deliberately target veterans, single parents and people on unemployment benefits, whose federal aid the company can capture.

Students who try to withdraw are told they will lose all their aid and must repay it at once, which is not true. Complaints to the student services team are closed without action. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and the Department of Education has not been told.

brief:
Sentinel Custodial Services Ltd is a private detention contractor headquartered in Birmingham, England. It was founded in 2009 and runs four immigration removal centres in England under contracts with the Home Office, holding about 1,900 people at a time. It employs about 2,700 people. The people it holds include asylum seekers and others awaiting decisions on their immigration status, and its centres are inspected by HM Inspectorate of Prisons.

The company's profits depend on cutting costs below what its contracts pay for. Its centres have about half the nurses and doctors the contracts require, so detainees with diabetes, epilepsy and mental illness often go days without medication. Detainees who protest or refuse food are held in isolation rooms for days at a time as punishment, which is not allowed. Staff are told to fill in the hourly welfare-check logs for people at risk of suicide in advance, whether or not the checks happen, and two people have died in the past year after checks were missed.

Complaints from detainees and their lawyers are delayed until after people have been removed from the country. Staff who report abuse are moved to night shifts or dismissed. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and the Home Office and HM Inspectorate of Prisons have not been told.
